challenges.name: locks-alter-table-quiz
challenges.title: Read the lock queue
challenges.description: Three statements about the two minutes when a millisecond migration stopped every query on the orders table. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: Check the lock conflict table: does ACCESS SHARE (held by a SELECT) conflict with another SELECT's ACCESS SHARE? Then ask what a new request does when an earlier request in the queue is still waiting.
Look up the volatility of `now()`: is it evaluated per row or once per statement, and what does PostgreSQL 11 and later store for a non-volatile default?
Read the error message and the timestamps: what did the migration do while the report query held its lock, and what did the other queries do meanwhile?

questions.question:
The incident, two minutes after the migration started:

```text
-- pg_stat_activity (abridged)
  pid  | state  | wait_event_type | wait_event | duration | query
 50211 | active |                 |            | 00:02:04 | SELECT ... FROM orders JOIN ... -- weekly report
 50388 | active | Lock            | relation   | 00:01:58 | ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer DEFAULT 0
 50401 | active | Lock            | relation   | 00:01:57 | SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1
 50417 | active | Lock            | relation   | 00:01:57 | INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...)
 ... 212 more rows waiting on relation orders
```

Statement: "Only the `ALTER TABLE` was blocked by the migration; the `SELECT` and `INSERT` sessions were waiting for the report query and would have waited just as long without the migration."
questions.explanation: False. The report holds ACCESS SHARE, which conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE: without the migration, other SELECTs and INSERTs run next to it. The `ALTER TABLE` asked for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and queued behind the report. Every later request that conflicts with the waiting ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (every request, even a plain SELECT) queued behind the `ALTER TABLE`. A statement that needs milliseconds of work stopped the whole table for as long as the report ran.

questions.question:
On PostgreSQL 17, the production `orders` table has 18 million rows:

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN accepted_at timestamptz DEFAULT now();
-- ALTER TABLE
-- Time: 3.104 ms
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE accepted_at IS NULL) FROM orders;
--  0
```

Statement: "`now()` gives every row its own value, so PostgreSQL must rewrite all 18 million rows; a timing of 3 ms means the command did not run against the real table."
questions.explanation: False. `now()` is a stable function: it returns the start time of the current transaction, evaluated once for the whole statement. Since PostgreSQL 11, a column added with a non-volatile default stores that one value in the catalog and serves it for every existing row, without rewriting them; that is why the count of NULLs is 0 after 3 ms. A volatile default such as `clock_timestamp()` or `gen_random_uuid()` would rewrite the table.

questions.question:
The team now runs every migration with a lock timeout and retries:

```text
migrate  SET lock_timeout = '3s'
migrate  ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer DEFAULT 0
migrate  ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
migrate  attempt 1 failed, retrying in 20s
migrate  ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer DEFAULT 0
migrate  ALTER TABLE  (Time: 2.871 ms)
```

Statement: "The `ALTER TABLE` gave up after waiting 3 seconds for its lock instead of making every query queue behind it for minutes; the retry found a moment when no conflicting lock was held."
questions.explanation: True. `lock_timeout` aborts a statement that waits longer than the limit to acquire a lock. Other queries can queue behind it for those 3 seconds at most, and the migration tool tries again later, when the long query has finished. The timeout must be short enough that 3 seconds of queued queries are acceptable; `statement_timeout` alone does not help, because it also counts the work, not only the wait.

challenges.name: migration-linter
challenges.title: Fix the migration linter
challenges.description: Rice Rocket's CI runs `tools/lint_migrations.py` on every migration. It passed the `ALTER TABLE` that stopped the orders table, called a `gen_random_uuid()` default safe, told a developer to wrap `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in a transaction (which PostgreSQL refuses), and flagged `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` as blocking. The editor holds the linter with its rule blocks missing, each marked by a `# [ ]` line; some pieces are last month's buggy rules. Fill every line so that `lint(statements, pg_version)` reports, for each statement, the lock PostgreSQL takes, the work it does, a verdict, and the statements to run instead, following the rules in the module's docstring. Run lints sample migrations against PostgreSQL 17 and 10.
hints: For each statement ask two questions: which lock, and for how long? A lock that blocks writes is fine for a catalog change (with a lock timeout) and not fine for a scan, rewrite or index build.

Look at the volatile function check in `default_rewrites`, at what a migration tool does with `BEGIN` / `COMMIT` around `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, and at the lock level of `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` in the ALTER TABLE documentation.

A linter rule for `CLUSTER orders USING orders_pkey` (rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) would read: `if re.match(r"cluster\b", low): return finding(s, "ACCESS EXCLUSIVE", "rewrites the table", "unsafe", ["-- use pg_repack or a new table"])`, placed before the generic ALTER TABLE parsing.

tests.name: The incident's ADD COLUMN with a constant or now() default: catalog only, needs lock_timeout

statements: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer DEFAULT 0;
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN accepted_at timestamptz DEFAULT now()

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer DEFAULT 0
fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer DEFAULT 0

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN accepted_at timestamptz DEFAULT now()
fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN accepted_at timestamptz DEFAULT now()

tests.name: A volatile default rewrites the table and is split into add, set default and backfill

statements: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN public_id uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN public_id uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN public_id uuid
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN public_id SET DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
-- backfill existing rows in batches

tests.name: CREATE INDEX blocks writes; the fix builds it concurrently, outside any transaction

statements: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_public_id_key ON orders (public_id)

fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_courier_id_idx ON orders (courier_id)

expected.sql: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_public_id_key ON orders (public_id)
fix: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_public_id_key ON orders (public_id)

tests.name: A foreign key is added NOT VALID, then validated under a lock that lets writes through

statements: ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_courier_fk FOREIGN KEY (courier_id) REFERENCES couriers (id)
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_courier_fk

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_courier_fk FOREIGN KEY (courier_id) REFERENCES couriers (id)
fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_courier_fk FOREIGN KEY (courier_id) REFERENCES couriers (id) NOT VALID
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_courier_fk

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_courier_fk
fix: ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_courier_fk

tests.name: SET NOT NULL through a CHECK constraint, a type change, a rename and a drop

statements: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN restaurant_id SET NOT NULL
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN total_vnd TYPE bigint
ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN note TO customer_note
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN legacy_status

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN restaurant_id SET NOT NULL
fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_restaurant_id_not_null CHECK (restaurant_id IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_restaurant_id_not_null
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN restaurant_id SET NOT NULL
ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_restaurant_id_not_null

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN total_vnd TYPE bigint
fix: -- expand and contract: add a new column, backfill in batches, switch reads, drop the old one later

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN note TO customer_note
fix: -- expand and contract: add a new column, backfill in batches, switch reads, drop the old one later

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN legacy_status
fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN legacy_status

tests.name: On PostgreSQL 10 any default rewrites and SET NOT NULL has no shortcut

statements: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer DEFAULT 0
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN restaurant_id SET NOT NULL

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer DEFAULT 0
fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN tip_vnd integer
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN tip_vnd SET DEFAULT 0
-- backfill existing rows in batches

expected.sql: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN restaurant_id SET NOT NULL
fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN restaurant_id SET NOT NULL
VACUUM orders
